Chapter 0180 BPMPROCESSING

The Morning Meeting

Before sunrise, someone feeds the crows at Trout Lake. That is the whole meeting.

Every morning before the sun, a thin mist lies on Trout Lake, and the day's first meeting happens where almost nobody sees it. If you walked past you would see a murder of crows in a tree by the water and one weathered street artist on a bench, paint on their hands, feeding them. That is the whole meeting. The crows are reporting: they spent yesterday over the roofs, wires, walls and parks and noticed which corners have gone quiet and where music, art and attention are running thin. They do not speak English. The painter understands anyway. No chairperson, no agenda, no minutes. The meeting decides what the city needs today.

Before sunrise, the painter takes the same lane toward Trout Lake. The bucket brushes a trouser leg. Above the roofs, crows lift off one at a time. A thin mist finds its own way between the houses. All three are going to the same place.

At the park, the painter joins the others: a roller on a shoulder, a cart, a skateboard, a bicycle with a bucket on the bars. They fall into step without saying good morning. At the water, the painter takes the bench. The others wait beneath the trees while the crows settle close enough to be fed.

Yesterday they inspected the whole city. This morning, among the roofs and wires briefly reflected in the lake, there is a new courtyard. People have moved in. The walls are still bare. A person with a cup pauses at the entrance, then keeps walking. A bench waits at the far end, and sound seems to pass the entrance without turning in. Behind the new walls stands an old brick doorway that nobody looks toward.

The painter stops feeding for a moment. Under the trees, the second painter shifts the roller on her shoulder.

Then the crows leave. The crew picks up its things. To anyone passing, it was a person feeding birds while some painters waited. The mist is already finding the way out.

The ruleIf it looks like a person feeding crows, the meeting is probably going well.

Terminal City · Storybook v0.9.0 · built 2026-09-12
Terminal City is an original fictional mythology inspired by Vancouver’s geography, weather, wildlife, infrastructure, art, and electronic music. It makes no claim to historical, Indigenous, or religious tradition. Real places are used as settings; the operating system layered on them is invented.
Made by Steve Hiehn, a software developer and electronic musician based in Vancouver, Canada. All music was created using a custom DAW, Signals & Sorcery.
